nodes.en: A Buddhist amulet, usually a small moulded image of a Buddha or revered monk.
The Somdej amulet — among the most revered Thai amulet types, the 'king of amulets.'
Jatukham Ramathep — a guardian-deity amulet cult that swept Thailand in the 2000s.
A spell inscribed on a thin metal scroll, rolled tight and empowered — worn for protection, invulnerability, or love.

nodes.l: เครื่องราง
nodes.en: Talisman or charm, in the broad sense — any empowered object worn or carried for its power.
Auspicious sacred objects — the umbrella category for amulets, charms and consecrated items.
The eclipse-deity — the shadow-planet that swallows sun and moon; propitiated to turn misfortune to fortune.

nodes.l: โหราศาสตร์
nodes.en: Astrology — the reckoning of time, star and fate; the diviner's science of auspicious days and birth-charts.

nodes.l: เมตตามหานิยม
nodes.en: Loving-kindness + 'great popularity' — charm that makes one widely liked and favoured.
Loving-kindness — as a magical quality, the power to draw goodwill and warmth from all who meet you.

nodes.l: สีผึ้งเสน่ห์
nodes.en: Enchanted lip-wax — a balm consecrated to lend the wearer allure.
Love-drawing allure — charms and rites to kindle desire and attraction.

nodes.l: ท้าวเวสสุวรรณ
nodes.en: Vaishravana — guardian king of the north, giant lord of yakṣas, who wards off ghosts and evil.

Buddho, 'the Awakened One' — the commonest meditation word of the Thai forest tradition (bud- on the in-breath, -dho on the out-breath) and a seed-word in katha; with dhammo and saṅgho it makes the Triple-Gem triad.
A Pali incantation — verses of power, recited to activate a charm, ward danger, or draw fortune.
Buddhaṃ — 'the Buddha' as the object of the refuge formula: buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, 'I go to the Buddha for refuge'. The three refuge lines open almost every rite in the corpus.
Dhammaṃ — 'the Dhamma' in the second refuge line: dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.
Saṅghaṃ — 'the Sangha' in the third refuge line: saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.
'Homage' — the first word of the salutation (namo tassa bhagavato…), and the word with which a katha, a recipe, or a rite begins.

nodes.l: นะโมพุทธายะ
nodes.en: 'Homage to the Buddha' — the five-syllable formula na-mo-phut-tha-ya, the commonest katha in the corpus. Tradition holds each syllable stands for one of the five Buddhas of this aeon (พระเจ้าห้าพระองค์); inscribed in yantra as a 5-cell row, rotated and reversed in consecration.
Dhammo, 'the Teaching' — recited as the second of the Triple-Gem triad (buddho dhammo saṅgho).

Itipiso — the opening of the recollection of the Buddha's qualities (itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho…). The katha tradition recites it, reverses it, counts it (Itipiso 108) and lays its syllables out as yantra.
Arahaṃ, 'the Worthy One' — first of the nine qualities of the Buddha; also breathed as a two-beat meditation word (a-ra-haṃ) and used as a seed in protective katha.
Saraṇaṃ, 'refuge' — the word at the centre of each refuge line.
Upekkhā, 'equanimity' — fourth of the four brahmavihāra.

The four-syllable 'heart of the elements' — na, ma, pha, tha, one for each of earth, water, fire and wind. Written into 4×4 yantra squares and read forward and backward (anuloma / patiloma) while a charm is empowered.
The three syllables ma-a-u — the 'heart of the Triple Gem' (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) in Thai esoteric use; the same three sounds as Om (a-u-ma), reordered.
Bhagavā, 'the Blessed One' — the Buddha's epithet and the second word of the Itipiso; often stands alone in a yantra cell as a seed-word.
Sabbe, 'all' — opens the loving-kindness and protective formulae (sabbe sattā… 'may all beings…'), which the manuscripts recite over water, oil and the body.
Ehi, 'come!' — the summoning imperative that opens katha of calling: customers, lovers, spirits, fortune (ehi… piyaṃ mama).

nodes.l: สิทธิการิยะ
nodes.en: 'May it be accomplished' — the auspicious word with which a Thai manuscript, recipe or formula opens; the scribe's invocation, and the marker that a new text is beginning.
Karuṇā, 'compassion' — second of the four brahmavihāra (mettā karuṇā muditā upekkhā), recited in sequence as a blessing and named among the qualities a charm bestows.
'Of the Blessed One' — the form heard in the salutation namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.
Saṅgho, 'the Community' — third of the Triple-Gem triad.
Gacchāmi, 'I go' — the verb that closes each refuge line.

nodes.l: สิทธิกิจจัง
nodes.en: 'May the task succeed' — from the success-blessing siddhikiccaṃ siddhikammaṃ siddhikāriya tathāgato, recited to seal a rite or a making.
Dukkhaṃ, 'suffering' — with aniccaṃ (impermanence) and anattā (not-self) one of the three marks; recited as a contemplation formula and used as a seed in katha.
Muditā, 'sympathetic joy' — third of the four brahmavihāra.
Namāmihaṃ, 'I pay homage' — the closing word of many salutation-katha (… namāmihaṃ).
Anattā, 'not-self' — third of the three marks (aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā).
The sacred syllable นะ — a seed-letter at the heart of countless katha and yantra; the tradition counts 108 of its forms.

nodes.l: พญาเต่าเรือน
nodes.en: The turtle amulet — for longevity and steady, sheltering wealth.
A phallic amulet — carved for protection, virility and warding of harm.
A cowrie-shell remedy charm — the classic guard against black magic and curse.

nodes.l: กะลาตาเดียว
nodes.en: A rare one-eyed coconut shell — a single natural sprout-hole makes it a powerful protective charm.

nodes.l: เขี้ยวเสือ
nodes.en: Tiger fang — worn for authority, command over others and protection.
Medicine — herbal remedy and the medical manuals; healing sits inside wichaa, not apart from it.
Invulnerability — the classic martial protection, skin that blades cannot cut.
Sacred powder of Buddha-virtue — ground from consecrated materials and pressed into amulets.
Chewed betel-quid — spat and worked into folk blessing, healing and love magic.

nodes.l: น้ำมันมนต์
nodes.en: Enchanted oil — consecrated for love, luck or persuasion, anointed on skin or object.
The ritual master's knife — for exorcism, cutting malign influence, and consecrating charms.
To cultivate by recitation — repeating a katha, in the mind or aloud, a set number of times to charge a charm or oneself; the manuscripts' verb for 'recite / meditate on'.
Candle — offering and instrument both: candles of set weight and number open the rite, and their flame or dripping wax carries the consecration.
The precepts (sīla — five or eight) — the moral discipline the manuscripts set alongside recitation as its condition.
To consecrate by spell — breathe a katha over water, oil, wax, powder or an amulet to empower it. The central verb of the craft.
A count of recitations — 'recite 3 คาบ, 7 คาบ, 108 คาบ'; the unit in which the manuscripts measure a katha's work.
Incense stick — counted out in set numbers (3, 5, 9, 16…) as the offering that opens a rite and honours the teacher-line.
The 'golden boy' — a child-spirit effigy kept and fed for luck, wealth and protection.
The beckoning lady — her raised hand calls in customers and wealth; the merchant's charm.
Ai Khai — the boy-spirit of Wat Chedi, famed for granting luck and answered wishes.

nodes.l: หลวงปู่ทวด
nodes.en: A revered southern monk (16th–17th c.), whose amulets are believed to protect from harm and misfortune.
The ascetic hermit-seers — the teacher-figures at the root of the tradition, patrons of yantra, katha and healing.
A yantra inked onto cloth — a protective banner or wearing-cloth carrying the diagram.
A sacred diagram of letters, syllables and lines — drawn, inscribed or tattooed to protect, empower, or attract. The north's core visual magic.
